Approach

 

Q. What are 3 acquired causes of high HbA2 ( ie not other than hemoglobin variants running in A2)?

●      Megaloblastic anemia (B12 and folate def) - Ineffective erythropoiesis in megaloblastic anemia can lead to increased δ-globin synthesis, resulting in elevated HbA₂.

●      Hyperthyroidism - Increased erythropoietic activity due to thyroid hormone excess may alter globin chain synthesis, resulting in higher HbA₂ levels.

●      HIV therapy eg Zidovudine - Zidovudine affects erythropoiesis, leading to increased δ-globin synthesis and subsequent elevation of HbA₂.

●      (Beta-thal)

 

Q. What are 3 acquired causes of low HbA2

Essentially the “(T)AILS” mnemonic without the “T”

 

●      Anemia of chronic inflammation

●      IDA

●      Lead poisoning

●      Sideroblastic anemia

●      Hypothyroidism

●      Alpha Thal trait

●      Delta variants

●      HPFH

●      JMML

●      AML

●      AA

●      Acquired HbH disease

 

Q. What are 5 inherited causes of high HbA2?

·       Beta thal trait

·       Vietnamese / South-East Asian type deletional hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin (HPFH)

·       Hereditary high hemoglobin A2 with autosomal dominant inheritance

·       Hereditary high hemoglobin A2 resulting from a mutation in the promotor of the delta gene

·       Unstable hemoglobin

·       Sickle cell trait

·       Sickle cell anemia, particularly if there is coexisting alpha thalassemia

·       Sickle cell / beta0 thal

·       Heterozygosity for certain beta chain variants, eg. Hb Leslie

·       Congenital dyserythropoietic anemia

 

 

Q. What are 5 inherited causes of low HbA2?

·       Delta+ thal heterozygosity or homozygosity

·       Delta0 thal heterozygosity or homozygosity

·       Some cases of delta-beta0 thal heterozygosity and all cases of delta-beta0 thal homozygosity

·       Some cases of A-gamma-delta-beta thal heterozytosity and all cases of A-gamma-delta-beta0 thal homozygosity

·       Deletional hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin heterozygosity and homozygosity

·       Alpha thal trait and hemoglobin H disease

·       Hemoglobin Lepore heterozygosity, compound heterozygosity and homozygosity

·       Hemoglobin Kenya heterozygosity

·       Heterozygosity for delta chain variants

Acquired Causes of High HbF[QZ1] 

1. Adults or Any Age:

  • Pregnancy (15-20% of pregnancies; HbF can increase up to 5%)
  • Stress erythropoiesis
  • Aplastic anemia
  • Pernicious anemia
  • Hematological malignancies:
    • Acute myeloblastic leukemia
    • Myelodysplastic syndrome
    • Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)
    • Polycythemia vera
  • Tumors (e.g., choriocarcinoma, bronchial, breast, ovarian, gastrointestinal)
  • Thyrotoxicosis
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Starvation ketoacidosis
  • Kala azar (visceral leishmaniasis)
  • Drug-induced (e.g., erythropoietin, hydroxyurea, sodium valproate)

 

2. Childhood:

  • Juvenile Myelomonocytic Leukemia (JMML)

 

3. General Categories (All Ages):

A. Developmental Causes:

  • Trisomy 13
  • Premature birth
  • Small for gestational age infants
  • Chronic intrauterine hypoxia
  • Infants of diabetic mothers
  • Maternal smoking during pregnancy

B. Bone Marrow Regeneration:

  • Recovery following:
    • Transient erythroblastopenia of childhood (TEC)
    • Bone marrow transplantation
    • Chemotherapy
    • Severe iron deficiency anemia (IDA)
  • Erythroid expansion during pregnancy

C. Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes (though congenital, listed for comparison):

  • Fanconi anemia (FA)
  • Dyskeratosis congenita (DKC)
  • Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA)

D. Hematological Malignancies:

  • Juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML)
  • Erythroleukemia
  • Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS)
  • Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)
  • Polycythemia vera
  • Multiple myeloma

E. Miscellaneous:

  • Stress erythropoiesis:
    • Blood loss or severe phlebotomy
    • Acute or severe hemolysis
    • Recovery from bone marrow failure or aplasia
    • Post-infection or after iron therapy for IDA
    • Following marrow recovery in leukemia treatment
  • Medications:
    • Erythropoietin therapy
    • Hydroxyurea for sickle cell anemia or beta-thalassemia intermedia
    • Butyrate, 5-azacytidine, or sodium valproate therapy in hemoglobinopathies.

Q1: What is the consequence of substituting an external amino acid that is not involved in inter-chain contacts in globin genes?
A1: The substitution does not lead to any functional abnormality. An example is Hemoglobin G-Philadelphia.

 

Q2: What happens when an amino acid substitution leads to reduced solubility and polymerization of hemoglobin?
A2: It causes hemoglobin S (sickle cell hemoglobin), which leads to the deformation of red blood cells into a sickle shape, resulting in hemolysis and vascular obstruction.

 

Q3: How does an amino acid substitution that leads to reduced solubility affect hemoglobin?
A3: It causes hemoglobin C, where the substitution leads to the formation of straight-edged crystals in red blood cells, causing hemolysis.

 

Q4: What is the result of replacing a histidine residue involved in hemoglobin binding with another amino acid?
A4: This mutation increases the tendency for hemoglobin to oxidize, forming methemoglobin. Cyanosis may occur from birth if the mutation is in a γ gene, from birth with an α chain defect, or from around 6 months if the defect is in a β chain. There may also be associated hemoglobin instability.

 

Q5: What occurs when mutations involve amino acids in the hemoglobin pocket or affect tetrameric contacts?
A5: These mutations, such as in hemoglobin Köln, hemoglobin Zurich, or hemoglobin Kansas, lead to hemoglobin instability and Heinz body hemolytic anemia. There may also be decreased oxygen affinity and resultant cyanosis.

 

Q6: What is the consequence of mutations affecting 2,3-DPG interaction or tetrameric hemoglobin contacts?
A6: Mutations in the a1b2 or a2b1 tetrameric contacts, or the C-terminal end of the β chain, lead to increased oxygen affinity and polycythemia. Examples include hemoglobin Chesapeake, hemoglobin Bethesda, and hemoglobin Yakima.

 

Q7: What happens when there is a mutation that decreases oxygen affinity in hemoglobin?
A7: This mutation leads to anaemia because oxygen delivery to tissues is maintained with a lower hemoglobin concentration, which can also cause cyanosis. Examples include hemoglobin S, hemoglobin Seattle, and hemoglobin Kansas.

 

Q8: What is the effect of a mutation in the β-globin gene that leads to markedly reduced or absent β chain production?
A8: This results in β-thalassemia (major, intermedia, or minor), where the reduced synthesis of hemoglobin A leads to ineffective erythropoiesis and damage to developing erythroblasts due to the accumulation of excess α chains.

 

Q9: What happens when there is a mutation in the β-globin gene leading to a structurally abnormal and unstable β chain?
A9: This results in a dominant β-thalassemia phenotype, where the β chain is unstable, and the mutation leads to abnormal hemoglobin.

 

Q10: What is the consequence of a mutation in the α-globin gene that markedly reduces or completely abolishes α chain synthesis?
A10: This causes α-thalassemia, leading to reduced synthesis of hemoglobin F, A, and A2. Severe cases may lead to hemoglobin H disease or hemoglobin Bart’s hydrop fetalis.

 

Q11: What occurs when there is a mutation in the α-globin gene that leads to a structurally abnormal α chain?
A11: This results in a α-thalassemia phenotype, such as hemoglobin Constant Spring, where α chain synthesis is greatly reduced.

 

Q12: What happens if there is a mutation in the δ-globin gene leading to abnormal structure or reduced production?
A12: This results in a hemoglobin A2 variant or δ-thalassemia. While there is no significant clinical effect since hemoglobin A2 is a minor hemoglobin, it can complicate the diagnosis of thalassemia trait.

 

Q13: What is the effect of a mutation in the γ-globin gene that causes structural abnormalities or reduced synthesis of γ chains?
A13: This leads to some methaemoglobins and can affect the synthesis of hemoglobin F (fetal hemoglobin), which may cause clinical symptoms in some cases.

 

Q1: What is the expected proportion of an α-chain variant in the blood?
A1: The proportion of an α-chain variant might typically be around 25%, as there are usually four α-globin genes. However, this proportion can be higher or lower depending on several factors.

 

Q2: How does the mutation of the α2 gene affect the proportion of an α-chain variant?
A2: If the α-chain variant results from a mutation of the α2 gene, the proportion can be more than 25%, since the normal ratio of α2 to α1 synthesis is around 3:1, favoring α2. This results in a higher proportion of the variant.

 

Q3: How does the mutation of the α1 gene affect the proportion of an α-chain variant?
A3: If the α-chain variant results from a mutation of the α1 gene, the proportion of the variant is less than 25%, due to the reduced synthesis of α1 chains.

 

Q4: How does co-inheritance of α-thalassemia affect the proportion of an α-chain variant?
A4: Co-inheritance of α-thalassemia leads to a lower percentage of the variant α-chain, as α-thalassemia reduces the total amount of normal α chains.

 

Q5: What happens if a mutated α1 gene is in cis with the deletion of the α2 gene?
A5: If a mutated α1 gene is in cis with a deletion of the α2 gene, the variant α-chain may be upregulated, increasing the proportion of the variant in the blood.

 

Q6: How does reduced synthesis or instability affect the percentage of the variant α-chain?
A6: The percentage of the variant α-chain is reduced if the variant is synthesized at a reduced rate, if it has lower affinity for β chains than normal α chains, or if the variant is unstable.

 

Q7: What is the expected proportion of a β-chain variant in the blood?
A7: In heterozygotes, a β-chain variant might represent around 50% of total hemoglobin, as there are two β-globin genes.

 

Q8: How do negatively charged β chains affect the proportion of a β-chain variant?
A8: Variants with negatively charged β chains (such as hemoglobin J-Baltimore or J-Iran) have a greater affinity for α chains than normal β chains, leading to an increased proportion of the variant hemoglobin, which may be above 50%.

 

Q9: How does co-inheritance of α-thalassemia affect the proportion of a β-chain variant with negatively charged chains?
A9: Co-inheritance of α-thalassemia, which results in a lack of α chains, increases the proportion of the variant β chain with negatively charged variants.

 

Q10: How do positively charged β chains affect the proportion of a β-chain variant?
A10: Positively charged β chains, such as βS, βC, βO-Arab, and βD-Punjab, have a lower affinity for α chains, leading to a reduced proportion of the variant β chain, typically below 50%.

 

Q11: How does co-inheritance of α-thalassemia affect the proportion of positively charged β-chain variants?
A11: If there is co-inheritance of α-thalassemia, the proportion of the positively charged β-chain variant will be even lower due to the lack of α chains.

 

Q12: What happens if the synthesis of a β-chain variant is reduced or unstable?
A12: The percentage of the β-chain variant will be reduced if there is a reduced rate of synthesis of the variant β chain (e.g., βE, βLepore) or if the β chain is unstable (e.g., hemoglobin Köln).

Q. What is a Mentzer index?

●      A calculation which is supposed to help distinguish IDA from beta thalassemia (validated for beta thal only → not alpha thal)

●      It is the MCV/RBC count.

●      If less than 13 thalassemia is more likely.

●      If more than 13 IDA is more likely.

○      Eg 60/6.4 = 9.3 → suggests thal

○      Eg 60/4.2 = 14.3 → suggests IDA

●      Some people say 13-17 is equivocal.

 

Q. Alpha thal vs beta thal basic pathophysiology?

●      Alpha thalassemia is due to impaired production of alpha globin chains, leading to a relative excess of beta globin chains.

●      The toxicity of the excess beta globin chains on the red cell membrane skeleton appears to be less than that of the excess partially oxidized alpha globin chains in beta thalassemia.

●      Beta tetramers (alpha thal) = less harmful than alpha tetramers (beta thal)

Q. What is alpha0 and what is alpha+ thalassemia?

·       Alpha0: Deletion of both HBA genes on the same chromosome, referred to as α0-thalassemia or cis deletion α-thalassemia, results in a greater degree of chain imbalance, since there is a 50% decrease in HBA expression. (cis genotype αα/--)

·       Alpha+: aka trans deletion α-thalassemia, Loss of one of four α-globin genes (genotype αα/-α) may result in a low-normal mean corpuscular volume (MCV)  and/or mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH); loss of one gene from each chromosome (trans genotype -α/-α) results in a MCV of 75–80 fL, and there is generally little to no anemia.

Q. What is the difference between deletional vs nondeletional alpha thal?

·       Deletional alpha thal results in either alpha0 or alpha+ thal.

·       Nondeletional alpha thal usually leads to alpha+ thal trait -> Hb Constant Spring

·       Nondeletional can result from mutations of a2 gene (aTa thal) or a1 gene (aaT thal), the former has a much more severe phenotype, because there is no upregulation of a1 gene. Most common nondeletional thal is Hb Constant Spring.

 Q. Four reasons predicting percentage of an alpha chain variant is difficult?

 

●      There are 4 alpha chains total; 2 on each chr 16

○      A2 makes up 75% of alpha chains & A1 makes up 25%

●      An A1 variant would expect to represent 12.5% of hemoglobin and an A2 variant 37.5%.

●      These expected %’s may differ because:

1. The variant chain may be produced at a reduced rate

2. The variant may have greater or lesser affinity for beta chains

3. The variant may be unstable

4. There may be a coexisting alpha or beta thalassemia

 

Q. Alpha thalassemia geographic location

●      Predominantly southeast Asia (SEA) and Africa

 

Q. Alpha thalassemia general classification? Explain the genotype for each of the following in alpha thalassemia: silent carrier, trait, HbH disease, constant spring and alpha thal major

 

●      1 mutated/deleted = asymptomatic/silent carrier

●      2 mutated/deleted = alpha thal minor (trait)

○      a+ haplotype (-a/-a) (trans)

○      a0 haplotype (--/aa) (cis)

●      3 mutated/deleted = HbH disease (intermedia) (--/-a) (Constant Spring is amino acid additions at α gene point 141-172[QZ3] )

●      All 4 genes deleted or mutated (--/--) = alpha thal major (hemoglobin Barts hydrops fetalis)

Q. What is meant by the terms “alpha thal type 1” and “type 2” (aka haplotype 1 and 2)?

●      Type 1 = A0 (--/aa) = cis

●      Type 2 = A+ (-a/-a) = trans

 

Q. Alpha thalassemia in Africans epidemiology - a+ or a0 more common?

●      28% are alpha thal trait haplotype a+ (-a/-a); a0 haplotype is virtually non-existent

●      a0 haplotype (--/aa) is common in southeast Asia, middle east, and Mediterranean populations

 

Q. What are rare causes of thalassemia outside of the hemoglobin alpha and beta chain genes?

 

●      Mutations in the upstream regulatory genes LCRA and LCRB (locus control region alpha and beta)

●      ATR-X (Alpha Thalassemia and Mental Retardation - X Chromosome)

○      Can be inherited, or acquired (as in AT- MDS)

○      Trans acting modifier

 

Q. Alpha thal minor (2 chain deletions) vs silent carrier - how do they differ in terms of clinical symptoms and CBC parameters?

●      Silent:

○      Affected subjects are clinically normal (silent) and may also be hematologically normal (normal CBC)

○      The diagnosis can be reliably made only via DNA analysis (PCR)

○      1 mutated/deleted gene

●      Minor:

○      These subjects are clinically normal but may have minimal anemia along with reductions in mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH).

○      Subjects may also have normal CBC indices though

○      2 mutated/deleted gene

 

Q. How to distinguish alpha thal silent carrier (a-/aa) vs minor (a-/a- or aa/--) on electrophoresis?

 

●      Both normal as adults.

●      Can only be differentiated at birth → by relative increase in Hb Barts

●      At birth:

○      Silent carrier is < 3% Hb Barts

○      Minor is 3-8% Hb Barts at birth

 

Q. What is alpha thalassemia mental retardation syndrome ATR-X - what is the gene involved, what chromosome is it located on?

●      X-linked syndrome → that affects males and causes a variety of features including mental retardation and alpha thalassemia

●      Mutations affecting the ATRX gene on the X chromosome are associated with the alpha thalassemia/mental retardation syndrome.

●      Trans acting gene modifier (ATRX)

●      Same gene affected in acquired alpha thal → eg MDS

Also: ATR16, large deletions of chromosome 16 (intellectual disability, microcephaly, alpha thal)

 

Q. Mechanism of anemia in alpha thal?

●      Decreased production of alpha globin

●      Imbalance of alpha and beta globin chains → excess beta globin chains

●      When alpha chains are underproduced the excess beta chains tetramerize and form Hb H bodies which are soluble but unstable and thus denature and precipitate as the cell ages (less intramedullary hemolysis than beta thal with fessas bodies)

●      This leads to increased deformability and subsequent removal by spleen = extravascular hemolysis

●      HbH bodies = less significant than fessas bodies (alpha tetramers in Beta thal)

 

When molecular testing is requested for alpha thalassemia, seven common alpha-globin gene deletions are typically screened for. These deletions are associated with varying clinical presentations and are prevalent in specific populations:

·       The single gene deletion detected in the study was -α.3.7 and -α.4.2, while the double gene deletion identified were —SEA, —FIL, —MED, and -α.20.5

HBH

Q. What is the blood film of hemoglobin H disease?

●      Hypochromic

●      Microcytosis

●      Striking polychromasia

●      marked poikilocytosis (tearsdrop cells, schistocytes, target cells, and elliptocytes)

●      Lacks marked increase in NRBCs seen with beta thal major

Q. Hemoglobin H properties?

●      B4 tetramers = HbH bodies

●      HbH can’t transport oxygen → high O2 affinity

●      Beta tetramers (HbH) are unstable so inclusion bodies form = HbH bodies

○      Extravascular hemolysis (RBCs containing HBH are removed by spleen) = variable degree of hemolytic anemia

○      Visible with supravital brilliant cresyl blue or new methylene blue staining (golf ball appearance)

 

Q. Differential for hemoglobin H inclusions (4) - ie what are 4 causes of HbH bodies seen on supravital stain?

●      Hemoglobin H disease

●      MPN - Myeloproliferative syndromes

●      AML - Erythroleukemia

●      MDS - Refractory sideroblastic anemia/MDS

 

Q. What is deletional vs non-deletional HbH disease?

 

●      Two general forms of HbH disease have been recognized.

●      1) Deletional form

○      The patient has inherited only a single alpha globin gene (ie, a-/--).

●      2) Non - deletional form

○      The patient has inherited two alpha globin genes from one parent, but one of these carries a non-deletional defect (ie, aa*/--)

○      Where a* represents the mutated alpha chain, such as hemoglobin Constant Spring, Quong Sze, or Hb Saudi

 

Q. What is more severe; deletional or non-deletional HbH disease?

●      HbH disease tends to be more severe in patients with the non-deletional form

●      Due, at least in part, to → interference with transcription of the normal alpha chain gene by the abnormal one

 

Q. Describe the Hb H disease findings for an adult on electrophoresis?

●      5 to 30% HbH present in adults (Bain: 1-40%, usually 8-10%)

●      20 to 40% Hb Barts at birth

 

Q. What are the clinical consequences of HbH associated with HbCS?

●      HbCS = Hb Constant Spring = a type of hemoglobin variant of the alpha gene that has an elongated alpha chain with 31 extra amino acids

●      Combination is severe and → often reliant on blood transfusion.

(A) Pattern of heterozygous Hb CS. (B-D) Pattern of homozygous Hb CS in an adult sample. (E) Pattern of homozygous Hb CS in a 5-day-old newborn. (F–G) Pattern of Hb H-CS in an adult sample.(H) Pattern of Hb H-CS in a newborn and infant.

 

Q. What is the issue related to the speed of Hgb H when doing gel electrophoresis?

●      If the presence of HbH is suspected, it is reasonable to reduce the length of time that electrophoresis is carried out →  in order to prevent HbH, if present, from completely running off the gel and be considered absent.

[QZ4] 

 

Summary of Hemoglobin Bart’s (γ₄) in Different α-Thalassemia Conditions (from Bain):

1.     Normal Neonates:

·       Hb Bart’s Level: 0.5–1.0%

·       Some healthy babies can have up to 1.2–2.6% Hb Bart’s.

2.     α⁺ Thalassemia (Single α-Globin Gene Deletion):

·       Heterozygous (–α/αα):

o   Hb Bart’s Level: 1–2%

o   May not always be present.

·       Homozygous (–α/–α):

o   Hb Bart’s Level: 3–10%

o   Overlap with heterozygous α⁺ cases.

3.     α⁰ Thalassemia Trait (Both α-Globin Genes Deleted on One Chromosome):

·        Genotype (– –/αα):

o   Hb Bart’s Level: 5–10%

o   Higher than in α⁺ thalassemia homozygotes.

o   Quantification by HPLC may show 7–11%.

4.     HbH (Three α-Globin Genes Deleted)

·        Genotype (– –/–α):

o   Hb Bart’s Level: 15-25%

o   Hb H 5-30% in adults

5.     Hb Bart’s Hydrops Fetalis (Deletion of All Four α Genes):

·        Genotype (– –/– –):

o   Hb Bart’s Level: 80–100%

o   Only γ₄ tetramers are formed; no functional α-globin is present.

o   Leads to severe fetal anemia and is usually fatal in utero.

CBC morphology in Hb Bart’s Hydrops Fetalis

 

Electrophoresis or high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC)

·        (₋α/αα): Silent carriers or α⁺ trait

o   Presence of Hb Bart's in very low concentrations between birth and 6 months; after 6 months, diagnosis requires molecular methods

·        (₋₋/αα) or (₋α/₋α): α⁰ trait

o   Newborns: Hb Bart's present up to 10%

o   After newborn period: Hb F, Hb A₂, and Hb A are normal

·        (₋₋/₋α): Hb H disease

o   Hb H up to 40%

o   Hb A₂ decreased

·        (₋₋/₋₋): Hb Bart’s

o   Hb Barts is fast-migrating (alkaline electrophoresis) and fast-eluting (HPLC) hemoglobin

o   Composed of gamma chain tetramers

o   Unstable and unable to deliver hemoglobin to tissues

o   In hydrops fetalis, 85-90% Hb Bart’s with no HbA and HbF

Beta thalassemia

Q. Beta thal geographic location?

●      Mediterranean, Middle East, India, Southeast Asia

 

Q. Why do excess alpha chains in beta thal cause clinical disease?

●      Beta thalassemia is due to impaired production of beta globin chains, leading to a relative excess of alpha globin chains.

●      Excess alpha globin chains are unstable, incapable of forming soluble tetramers on their own, and precipitate within the cell, causing oxidative membrane damage, leading to a variety of clinical manifestations (including intramedullary hemolysis).

Beta minor and intermedia

Q. Beta thal minor vs intermedia vs major genetic basis?

●      Beta thalassemia minor- These subjects are heterozygotes and carry one normal beta globin allele and one beta globin thalassemia allele. Aka beta thal trait.

●      Beta thalassemia intermedia – These subjects are compound heterozygotes for two different beta globin chain mutations

●      Beta thalassemia major – These severely affected subjects are homozygous for mutations associated with absent (or very severely reduced) production of beta chains.

●      Summary:

○      Minor → heterozygotes (one normal beta-globin allele and one mutated allele (either β⁰ or β⁺)

○      Intermedia → compound heterozygotes (two different beta-globin mutations, such as one β⁰ and one β⁺ allele, or two different β⁺ alleles)

○      Major → homozygous (either two β⁰ alleles, two β⁺ alleles, or one of each)

Q. Beta thalassemia minor CBC morphology

  • Microcytosis
  • Hypochromasia
  • Target cells
  • Basophilic stippling

 

Q. Describe beta thal minor and intermedia electrophoresis results?

●      HbA2 increased (3.5 to 7 percent)

●      HbF increased in about 50% of patients

Bain: However, if a patient has red cell indices suggestive of thalassaemia, but has a normal haemoglobin A2 percentage, it is essential to exclude elevation of haemoglobin F as db thalassaemia is an alternative diagnosis.

Q. Name 3 methods to accurately quantify A2?

●      HPLC

●      Capillary zone electrophoresis

●      Immunoaffinity chromatography (?microcolumn chromatography)

●      Cellulose acetate electrophoresis followed by elution and spectrophotometry

○      Only satisfactory if dealing with a small number (BB)

Q. What is the most common clinical phenotype for heterozygous beta thal mutations?

●      The vast majority of heterozygotes for beta thalassemia (eg, beta thalassemia trait) are asymptomatic.

 

Q. Why do the terms beta thal minor and intermedia exist?

 

●      The terms "beta thalassemia minor" and "beta thalassemia intermedia," attempt to reflect the fact that individuals carrying beta thalassemia mutations exhibit considerable clinical heterogeneity, requiring differences in approach to management.

●      Minor = asymptomatic without need for transfusion

●      Intermedia = symptomatic without need for regular transfusion (not transfusion dependent, which differentiates this group clinically from beta thal major).

○      Intermedia may develop increased requirements later in life

 

Q. What does the term beta thal intermedia typically refer to?

●      The term "beta thalassemia intermedia" (TI) refers to patients with symptomatic beta thalassemia who do not require transfusion during at least the first few years of life, and are able to survive into the second decade of life without chronic transfusion.

●      Note: These are now called NTDT (Non-transfusion dependent Thalassemias)

 

Additional questions

Q. Why is beta thal trait difficult to diagnose in neonates?

·       In neonates, HbA₂ levels are naturally low and not reliable for diagnosing β-thalassemia trait.

·       Diagnosis becomes clearer after 6–12 months, when HbA₂ levels increase and the decline in HbF is slower than in normal infants.

Q. What is the difference between silent and almost silent β-thalassemia?

  • Silent β-thalassemia trait: Normal red cell indices and HbA₂ levels. Requires genetic testing for diagnosis.
  • Almost silent β-thalassemia trait: Abnormal red cell indices (e.g., low MCV, MCH) but normal HbA₂ levels. Can resemble α-thalassemia trait.

Q. How do you differentiate β-thalassemia trait from iron deficiency anemia?

  • Both conditions cause microcytosis (low MCV), but in β-thalassemia trait, HbA₂ is elevated, whereas in iron deficiency anemia, HbA₂ is normal or slightly reduced.
  • Ferritin levels help differentiate the two.

Q. How does iron deficiency affect HbA₂ levels?

·        Iron deficiency can lower HbA₂ levels in both normal individuals and those with β-thalassemia trait.

Q. What about folic acid or vitamin B12 deficiency?

·        Folic acid deficiency: Lowers HbA₂ levels, complicating β-thalassemia diagnosis.

  • Megaloblastic anemia (due to B12 or folate deficiency): Typically increases HbA₂, proportional to the severity of anemia.

Q. What is the role of δ-thalassemia (δ⁰-thalassemia) in this context?

·        Coinheritance of δ-thalassemia (in cis or trans) with β-thalassemia can lead to normal HbA₂ levels, especially common in Sardinians and Cypriots.

Q. How does α-thalassemia coinheritance affect HbA₂ in β-thalassemia carriers?

·        Coinheritance of α-thalassemia (either heterozygous α⁰-thalassemia or homozygous α⁺-thalassemia) with mild β-thalassemia mutations can normalize both MCV and HbA₂ levels.

  • This combination can convert an almost silent thalassemia into a silent thalassemia, complicating the diagnosis.

Q. Can deletions of the upstream locus control region (LCR) affect HbA₂?

·        Yes, deletions affecting the LCR region can cause β-thalassemia with normal HbA₂ levels. This type of thalassemia is often missed without molecular genetic analysis.

Q. What happens when β-thalassemia heterozygosity coexists with HbH disease?

·        In cases of HbH disease (three α-gene deletions) and β-thalassemia, HbA₂ levels can be normal.

  • Reported Range: HbA₂ between 2.8% to 4.8%, often within the normal range.

Q. How can an A₂ variant interfere with diagnosis?

·        Some δ-globin chain variants can co-migrate with HbA₂ on HPLC or electrophoresis, leading to false normal readings. Failure to detect an A₂ variant (e.g., split A₂ bands) may result in missed β-thalassemia diagnosis.

Beta major

Q. Describe beta thal major electrophoresis results

●      HbA absent (HbA is alpha2/beta2 → can’t make beta → so can’t make HbA)

●      Only HbA2 and HbF are present

Q. What are the underlying causes of clinical effects in beta thal?

 

●      Effects of the profound anemia → due to ineffective erythropoiesis

●      Byproducts of hemolysis

●      Intramedullary and extramedullary expansion of erythroid marrow progenitors

○      EMH, bone deformity, osteoporosis/osteopenia, pathologic fractures

●      Long-term effects include:

○      The accumulation of end-organ damage → due to iron overload either from blood transfusions or accelerated iron absorption/turnover

○      Blood-borne infections (eg, viral hepatitis from blood transfusions), or

○      Progressive diversion of caloric resources to bone marrow expansion.

 

Q. How does beta thal major present?

●      Becomes clinically apparent during → the second six months of life, pallor, irritability, growth retardation, failure to thrive, abdominal swelling due to hepatosplenomegaly, and jaundice → reflect the onset and sequelae of severe hemolytic anemia.

●      The symptoms associated with ineffective erythropoiesis (eg, bony abnormalities and abnormal skeletal development) soon follow.

Q. Beta thalassemia major CBC morphology

o   Severe anaemia

o   Marked anisopoikilocytosis

o   Target cells

o   Basophilic stippling

o   Pappenheimer bodies

o   Numerous nRBCs

 

Q. What is the mortality of beta thal major?

●      Eighty percent (80%) of untreated children will die within the first 5 years of life

●      Death is due directly to the longer-term consequences of severe anemia, including high output heart failure, failure to thrive, lack of strength, and unusual susceptibility to infection

 

Q. Describe the skeletal changes in beta thal?

●      Skeletal abnormalities are dramatic in these patients and frequently lead to marked changes in the facial structure and body habitus, producing the characteristic "chipmunk facies" and delayed skeletal maturation.

●      Skeletal changes are due largely to the expansion and invasion of erythroid bone marrow → which widen the marrow spaces, attenuate the cortex, and produce osteoporosis.

●      Extramedullary hematopoiesis can actually break through cortex and behave like benign tumour in severe cases.

 

Q. What are common skull findings on x-ray in beta thalassemia?

●      Skull shows “hair-on-end” appearance and facial bones show “rodent facies”

 

Q. What is the role of RBC transfusion and transfusion thresholds in thalassemia major in pediatrics? Goals? Target Hb?

●      Transfusion is indicated to increase oxygen carrying capacity and suppress endogenous erythropoiesis that causes bony abnormalities.

●      Typically, transfused q3-4 weeks with pretransfusion of 95-105 and post transfusion of 130-135

 

Q. What accounts for variation in the clinical severity in beta thal major - patients with homozygous beta thal mutations - give three modulating factors?

 

Modulators of the phenotype of BTM include:

  1. Nature of the beta globin mutation
  2. Presence or absence of concurrent alpha globin mutations (presence will decrease the chain imbalance)
  3. Modulators of fetal hemoglobin production (HbF)

 

Q. What levels of HbF do you expect in homozygous beta thal?

●      Can range from 10% to 100%.

●      Usually lower in more mild alleles.

Q. What are the three types of hemoglobin Lepore and which is most common?

●      Lepore Boston [QZ6] = most common (also called Washington and Cyprus)

●      Lepore-Baltimore and

●      Lepore-Hollandia

 

Q. What are the differences in the different hemoglobin Lepore?

●      They only differ in their breakpoints.

 

Q. What is the molecular basis for hemoglobin Lepore?

●      The Hb Lepore syndrome arises from an unequal crossing over and recombination event between → delta and beta globin genes.

●      The result is production of a → fused (delta-beta) globin polypeptide.

 

Q. Why is hemoglobin Lepore thalassemic?

●      Because it is the result of a delta-beta fusion that is under the control of a delta globin promoter, which is only 2 to 3 % as active as the beta globin promoter

●      Due to the fusion, the beta gene ends up with a → shitty delta globin promoter

Q. What does hemoglobin Lepore look like on CBC and blood smear?

·        The blood count and blood film features cannot be distinguished from those of b thalassemia trait.

·        Hb A 78.3%

·        Hb A2 11.9% (Lepore migrates in A2; 5-15%)

·        Hb F 1.4%

·        5-15% Lepore, A2 reduced to half of normal reference level, mildly elevated F (Bain)

Hemoglobin Lepore Trait: HPLC

Hgb Lepore trait: Microcytosis (MCV 70-80) ; hemoglobin contains HbA, HbA2 (~2%), and variable amount of Hb F (1~14%) and Hb Lepore (5~15%)

Homozygous Lepore: Microcytic anemia; hemoglobin is made up of HbF and Hb Lepore only

 

Q. What is Hgb anti-Lepore and why is it not thalassemic?

●      Anti-Lepore is the other product of the unequal cross-over and recombination event between delta and beta globin genes that resulted in Hb Lepore

●      Hb anti-Lepore is the reciprocal (other) chromosome product of the unequal crossover events.

●      The anti-Lepore chromosome acquires a fused beta-delta chain which is under the control of the better functioning beta globin promoter. → therefore not thalassemic

●      Note: You also seem to have the normal intact delta and Beta on that chromosome along with the Anti-Lepore fusion gene

●      Variable types and lab properties

 

Q. What is the clinical phenotype of a homozygous hemoglobin Lepore?

●      Severe thalassemic disorder → similar to beta thal intermedia or major

●      30% Hb Lepore and 70% HbF

Q. What is the clinical significance of Hb Lepore and Hb S coinheritance

·       Hb 58, microcytic, hypochromic anemia

·       Alkaline gel: HbF, HbS, a slow moving Hb variant trailing HbS

·       HPLC: HbS 32%, HbA0 37%, HbF 15%, split A2 6% (note. HbA0 in this case represents the db-globin fusion chain from the Hb Lepore, not normal HbA. Retention time of Hb Lepore-Hollandia ovelaps with HbA2)

·       Hb Lepore-Hollandia mutation: NM_000518.4(HBB):c .-7305_92+16del (δ22Ala/β50Thr)

·       Compound heterozygosity for HbS/Hb Lepore-Hollandia.

·       The clinical severity of HbS-Lepore has been reported to vary with Lepore deletions.

Q. What is the molecular basis of Hgb Kenya and why does it cause increased fetal hemoglobin (HbF)?

 

●      Looks like HPFH with the presence of an added structural variant.

●      Results from an → unequal crossover and recombination event between the beta and A-Gamma globin genes.

●      This crossover produces a fused (A(gamma)-beta) gene.

○      So that your fusion would be Gamma-Beta (and the Gamma just happens to be of the A-gamma variety)

●      ? Presumably you get incr HbF because 1) you don’t have delta or beta and 2) the fused gene is under the control of the beta promoter?

Individuals with Hb Kenya usually exhibit:

●      Elevated HbF levels (often 20–40% or more) due to reduced beta globin production and compensatory gamma globin synthesis.

●      Symptoms depending on the degree of beta-globin deficiency and the level of compensatory HbF production.

●      The condition is generally classified as a thalassemia-like disorder due to the ineffective production of Hb A.

●       

 

Differential diagnosis of Lepore

 

Q-India

  • Mutation: α64 Asp→His in alpha-globin gene (benign alone).
  • Clinical: Asymptomatic carriers; compound heterozygotes (e.g., with beta-thalassemia) may develop moderate anemia.
  • Diagnosis: Electrophoresis/HPLC + DNA testing.
  • Significance: Prevalent in India; genetic counseling advised for at-risk couples.
  • Differential point: Q-India is not thalassemic like Lepore

Q. Hemoglobin C mutation?

·       Beta gene, codon 6, glutamic acid -> lysine

Q. Hemoglobin C disease - mcv and Hb?

●      Homozygous for C → 95% of hemoglobin is hemoglobin C.

●      Chronic, mild, hemolytic anemia.

●      Usually slightly microcytic.

Q. Hemoglobin C traits indices (MCHC, RDW, MCV)

●      MCHC slightly up

●      MCV slightly low

●      RDW increased

 

Q. What are PB and CBC findings in homozygous C?

 

●      Many target cells and hemoglobin C crystals (Washington monument shape) on PB

●      Mild to moderate hemolytic anemia with mild microcytosis on CBC.

Q. Where did hemoglobin C arise and what is it's benefit?

●      Appears to have arose in West Africa with up to 50% on the ivory coast having it and 40% in Burkina Faso.

●      Heterozygous protects against severe falciparum malaria and homozygous provides marked protection

●      Main issue is sickling with S trait

Q. Hb C/beta thal clinical findings

  • Hb C/β⁺-thalassemia
    • Predominantly found in Africa and in African Americans
    • Mild hemolytic anemia
    • Low Hb levels during pregnancy
  • Hb C/β⁰-thalassemia
    • In people of Mediterranean descent
    • Moderate to severe hemolytic anemia
    • Splenomegaly

Q. Hb C/beta thal laboratory findings

  • Hb C/β⁺-thalassemia
    • Microcytic anemia
    • Increased reticulocyte count
    • Peripheral smear shows increased target cells
    • Crystals not typically present
    • Hb C/β⁺-thalassemia
      • Predominance of Hb C (65-80%), Hb A (16-30%), and Hb F (2-5%)
  • Hb C/β⁰-thalassemia
    • Microcytic anemia
    • Increased reticulocyte count
    • Peripheral smear demonstrates predominance of target cells
      • Greater degree of anisopoikilocytosis than Hb CC disease
    • Hb C crystals not typically present but can be seen
    • Hb C/β⁰-thalassemia
      • Predominance of Hb C with mildly elevated Hb A₂ (3-8%) and Hb F (3-10%)
      • Hb A is absent

•        Inocuous, no anemia, slight microcytosis, mildly thalassemic blood picture

·       Hg EE / Hb E disease: no A, E – 99%, about 1% F

·       E/β-thal: severe thalassemia similar to classic β-thal major

·       Unstable Hb E → Can form Heinz bodies under oxidative stress.

Q. What is the trimodal distribution of the variant hemoglobin E in alpha thal?

·       Percentages of 29.1%, 27.3% and 17.4% correlating with the presence of four, three and two alpha globin genes, respectively (Bain)

·       Individuals with less than 25% of hemoglobin E almost always have coexisting a thalassemia trait

Q. Hemoglobin E mutation?

·       Beta gene, codon 26, glutamic acid -> lysine

Q. Hemoglobin E disease clinical manifestations?

●      Usually the patients are clinically asymptomatic in homozygous or heterozygous states.

Q. Why is Hb E Thalassemic?

●      The bE chain is synthesized at a reduced rate in comparison with bA.

●      It is decreased due to false/alternative splicing site towards the 3` end so a proportion is abnormally spliced → smaller amounts of beta globin mRNA are produced → underproduction of beta variant compared to normal = thalassemic

●      As a result indices can appear “thalassemic”

●      Therefore there are 2 causes of anemia in HbE

○      Decreased globin synthesis PLUS

○      Unstable Hb (heat & isopropanol stability tests are positive)

Q. Where is hemoglobin E most common?

●      Laos, Cambodia, and Thailand (the so-called "Hb E triangle”) where the trait approaches 50-60%

Q. HbE/β-Thalassaemia genotypes

·       HbE/β⁰: βE/β⁰: No HbA, HbF elevated (30–60%), HbE 40–60%; severe anemia, clinically resembles beta thal intermedia or major

·       HbE/β⁺: βE/β⁺: HbA present (~10%), HbE levels moderate, variable HbF; variable severity, ranging from mild anemia to transfusion dependency.

·       When Hb A is present, it usually is around 10% (Bain)

CBC morphology of E/beta thal

  • Moderate anaemia
  • Marked anisopoikilocytosis
  • Target cells
  • Basophilic stippling
  • Pappenheimer bodies
  • nRBCs vary in quantity from occasional to very frequent

Q. How to distinguish between haemoglobin E/β⁰-thalassaemia and haemoglobin E/β⁺-thalassaemia?

  • E/β⁰-thalassaemia: Presence of haemoglobins E, A₂, and F (NO beta NO HbA).
  • E/β⁺-thalassaemia: Presence of haemoglobins E, A, A₂, and F.
  •  Hgb E b0 thalassemia
  •  

Q. Other clinical variants of Hb E

Haemoglobin E with Haemoglobin H Disease

  • Heterozygous HbE with Haemoglobin H Disease:
    • Genotype: βE/βA with --/αα (or --/αCSα)
    • Clinical presentation: Similar to uncomplicated haemoglobin H disease, moderate anaemia, low MCV (52–67 fL).
    • Hb EA-Bart’s

  • Homozygous HbE with Haemoglobin H Disease:
    • Genotype: βE/βE with --/αα
    • Clinical phenotype: Severe thalassaemia intermedia with haemoglobin concentrations around 7–9 g/dL and low MCV (~61 fL).

Haemoglobin E with Bart’s Disease

  • Genotype: βE/βA with --/--
    • Bart’s haemoglobin (γ4 tetramers) predominates in newborns.
    • Severe anaemia due to a lack of α-globin chains.

Haemoglobin E with Haemoglobin Lepore

  • Genotype: βE/βLepore
    • Clinical phenotype: Significant anaemia resembling thalassaemia intermedia.

Haemoglobin E with Deletional Hereditary Persistence of Fetal Haemoglobin (HPFH)

  • Genotype: βE/HPFH
    • No clinical abnormality, but red cell indices may mimic thalassaemia trait.

Hb D (beta variant)

  1. Hemoglobin D (D-Los Angeles, D-Punjab)
    • Mutation: Substitution of glutamic acid (Glu) to glutamine (Gln) at β121 (DH4 position), same as in Hb O.
    • Ancestry:
      • Found in English, Irish, Scotch ancestry.
      • Uncommon in North America (AD < 1:5000).
      • India & Pakistan (Punjab): Approximately 3% of D trait in the population.
    • Clinical Forms:
      • Heterozygous Hb D trait (Hb AD):
        • Benign, no clinical symptoms.
        • Hematologically normal, with normal blood counts and blood films.
      • Homozygous Hb D disease (Hb DD):
        • Very rare.
        • Mild hemolytic anemia, usually no major complications.
        • May present with mild splenomegaly.
      • Hb D-β Thalassemia:
        • Mild to moderate hemolytic anemia.
        • May present with splenomegaly.
      • Hb SD Disease (Hb S/D Punjab):
        • Sickling disorder with moderate hemolytic anemia.
        • Clinically similar to sickle cell disease, but typically less severe than Hb SS.
  2. Hb D Characteristics
    • Normal Stability: Hb D has normal stability and normal or slightly increased oxygen affinity.
    • Blood Count in Hb D-Punjab trait: Typically normal unless coexisting alpha-thalassemia trait is present.
    • Blood Film: Normal in the absence of other conditions.
  3. Important Differential Hb Variants in Zone D
    • Beta variants:
      • Hb D-Iran
      • Hb Korle Bu
    • Alpha variants:
      • Hb G-Phil
    • Delta beta variants:
      • Hb Lepore (heterozygous forms show 5-15% Hb Lepore).

Q. Key features of Hb G trait (a2Gb2)

·       Most common a globin mutation

·       Do not sickle

·       Characteristics of an alpha globin mutation:

•        Expect 25% of major Hgb to be abnormal.

·       Alk: two bands, one in A and one in S (45%)

·       Acid: only one band in A

·       HPLC: Presence of Hgb A2 variant a2Gd2 detectable on HPLC

 

Q. Hemoglobin G-Philadelphia significance?

●      Has no clinical significance → but can cause diagnostic confusion.

●      G is an alpha variant

 

Q. What is important to note about hemoglobin G percentages?

 

It is commonly associated with alpha thalassemia. Levels are as follows:

1. G trait no alpha thal - 20-25%

2. G trait, and 1 alpha deletion - 25-35%

3. G trait and 2 alpha deletion - 35-45% and microcytosis

4. G homozygous and 2 alpha deletion - 95% and microcytosis

Percentage increases by 10% for each alpha thal (unlike E, decrease by 5% per alpha gene deletion)

Q. What does HbAS/G look like on alkaline and acid gel?

·       Alkaline pH (8.4–8.8)

o   Three bands:

o   Hemoglobin A (α₂β₂)

o   Hemoglobin S (α₂βS) and G-Philadelphia (αGβ₂): Co-migrate due to similar charge properties14.

o   S–G hybrid (αGβS): Migrates with hemoglobin C (βC), forming a distinct band.

·       Acid pH (Citrate Agar)

o   Two bands:

o   Hemoglobin A + G-Philadelphia: Both migrate together (αGβ₂ and α₂β₂ share mobility).

o   Hemoglobin S + S–G hybrid: α₂βS and αGβS co-migrate as a single S-like band.

·       HPLC Separation

o   four fractions emerge based on retention times: post‐translationally modified haemoglobin A (two peaks) and haemoglobins A0, A2, S, G‐Philadelphia and hybrid (ααGββS).

     haemoglobin A plus haemoglobin S plus haemoglobin G Philadelphia, the peaks from left to right being haemoglobin A (a2b2), G-Philadelphia (zone 6)(αG-Philaαb2), haemoglobin S (zone 5)(α2βS2), haemoglobin A2 (a2δ2), S-G hybrid (αG-Phil2βS2) (zone 2) and haemoglobin G2 (αG-Phil2δ2) (zone 1)

Q. What does HbSS/G look like on alkaline and acid gel?

  • two bands—one for HbS and a hybrid G-Philadelphia/S band, which migrates similarly to HbC at alkaline pH.
  • At acid pH, only one band is seen, resembling HbS.

 

Q. What is Hb G-Coushatta?

·       Hb G-Coushatta (HBB:c.68A>C) is a beta-globin variant in which an alanyl residue occurred in place of the glutamyl group at position 22.

·       It was first described in an American Coushatta Indian family.

·       Hb G-Coushatta elute in the Hb A2 window and could be mistaken for the common variants like Hb E and Hb D-Iran which also elute in the same window on HPLC.

Hb O (beta variant)

Mutation:

  • Beta-globin gene mutation: Substitution of glutamic acid (Glu) to lysine (Lys) at position 121 (GH4).

Prevalence:

  • Initially described in Arab individuals.
  • Common in the Balkans, Middle East, and Africa.
  • Trait prevalence: Approximately 0.4% in Bahrain; also reported in Bulgaria.

Clinical Features:

  1. Hb O-Arab Trait (Hb AO):
    • Clinically benign; no hematologic abnormalities.
    • No significant symptoms or health issues related to Hb O-Arab trait.
  1. Homozygous Hb O-Arab:
    • Very rare.
    • May present with hypochromia (low hemoglobin color) and microcytosis (small red blood cells), but no disability.
    • Generally asymptomatic despite abnormal hemoglobin.
  1. Hb S/Hb O-Arab (S/O-Arab):
    • This combination leads to severe sickling disorder (similar to Hb SS).
    • Severe clinical symptoms due to the presence of Hb S in combination with Hb O-Arab.

  1. Hb O-Arab with β-Thalassemia:
    • Mild to moderate anemia.
    • Jaundice and splenomegaly may be present.
    • Hemoglobin levels range from 60% to normal, with reduced MCV and increased reticulocytes.
    • Increased Hb F and Hb A2, possibly without Hb A.

Diagnostic Characteristics:

  • Percentage of Hb O-Arab in Trait: 38-43% of total hemoglobin.
  • Migration Patterns:
    • Alkaline pH: Migrates similar to C, between CEOA2.
    • Acid pH: Sits between Hb A and Hb S, but closer to Hb A.
    • HPLC (High Performance Liquid Chromatography): Retention time between Hb S and Hb C.
    • CZE (Capillary Zone Electrophoresis): Has distinct migration pattern from A2, useful for differential diagnosis.

Other Notable Hb O-Arab Variants:

  • Hb O-Arab/β-thalassemia Compound Heterozygote:
    • Can cause mild to moderate anemia.
    • Presents with jaundice and splenomegaly.
    • Hemoglobin levels around 6-8 g/dL.
    • Increased reticulocytes, reduced MCV, and slightly increased Hb F.

Clinical Impact Summary:

  • Trait: No symptoms.
  • Homozygous Hb O-Arab: Asymptomatic, but may present with mild microcytosis and hypochromia.
  • Sickle cell/Hb O-Arab: Severe sickling disorder.
  • Hb O-Arab/β-thalassemia: Presents with moderate anemia and splenomegaly.

•        Occurs in Asian ancestry

•        Target cells, microcytosis, elliptocytes

Hb Q-Thailand and HbH

Haemoglobin Q-H disease (--/-αQ) is caused by the co-inheritance of Hb Q-Thailand and α0 thalassaemia. The anaemia is usually moderate, with a thalassaemia intermedia phenotype.

Hb Q-Thailand is caused by a point mutation in the α globin gene. Most heterozygotes for Hb Q-Thailand have the genotype (αα/−αQ), and have a thalassaemia trait phenotype.

Blood film features:

  • The blood film looks similar to that of HbH disease
  • Marked hypochromic, microcytic anaemia
  • Anisopoikilocytosis with target cells, teardrop cells and fragments
  • Basophilic stippling
  • Polychromasia

Differential diagnosis:

  • Iron deficiency anaemia (degree of anisopoikilocytosis is too severe for isolated iron deficiency).
  • ß thalassaemia intermedia (such patients tend to have circulating nRBCs, which are absent in HbH disease. The reticulocytosis in HbH disease is also more prominent.).
  • Hereditary pyropoikilocytosis (cells are normocytic and haemoglobinization is normal).
  • Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemias (often characterised by macrocytosis with no reticulocytosis).
  • Acquired HbH disease (look for features of dysplasia, which may point towards an underlying myelodysplastic syndrome).

Haemoglobin electrophoresis:

·       Alkaline gel electrophoresis. There is a band with the mobility between that of haemoglobin F and haemoglobin S. A fast band corresponding to haemoglobin H.

·       Acid gel electrophoresis. It shows a variant haemoglobin with a mobility between Hb A and Hb S. This corresponds to Hb Q-Thailand. There is also a faint band with the same mobility of Hb A, likely representing Hb H.

·       The sickling test is negative in patients with haemoglobin Q.

HPLC:

·       There is no normal Hb A as there are no normal α chains. There are two variant haemoglobins. The first has a very short retention time, and corresponds to haemoglobin H (red arrow). The second (blue arrow) has a retention time of 4.66 minutes, falling in the S window. This represents haemoglobin Q-Thailand. The findings differ from that of sickle cell anaemia in that Hb H is not seen in sickle cell anaemia, and the mobility on acid gel especially is not the same as Hb S.

Haemoglobin Q-H Disease - LearnHaem | Haematology Made Simple

 

Alkaline cellulose acetate gel electrophoresis revealed two variants which migrated to the  Hb S/D/G position (aQ2g2) and a position slightly anodal to  Hb S/D/G position (aQ2b2), respectively (Fig. 2A); while on acid agarose gel electrophoresis, the two variants migrated to  a position between Hb A and Hb F (aQ2g2) and a position  slightly anodal to Hb S (aQ2b2), respectively (Fig. 2B).

Unstable Hemoglobins

Unstable hemoglobins are variant hemoglobins that lead to clinically recognizable hemolysis due to structural abnormalities.

156 variants in database; most are beta variants.

 

Key characteristics include:

Pathophysiology

  1. Structural Instability:
    • Mutations affect the secondary, tertiary, or quaternary structure.
    • Instability arises from:
      • Abnormalities in the heme pocket leading to heme loss.
      • Disruption of α-helical structures.
      • Substitution of non-polar with polar amino acids.
      • Weakening of α1β1 or α1β2 bonds.
      • Elongated β chains due to frameshift or stop codon mutations.
  1. Heinz Body Formation:
    • Precipitation of denatured hemoglobin (hemichromes).
    • Heinz bodies attach to red cell membranes, causing damage and loss of deformability.
  1. Clinical Presentation:
    • Hemolytic anemia ranging from mild to severe.
    • Jaundice and dark urine due to hemoglobin breakdown products.
    • Splenomegaly and increased gallstone risk.
    • Triggers for hemolysis: infections, oxidant drugs, or oxidative stress.
  1. Associated Abnormalities:
    • Altered oxygen affinity (increased or decreased).
    • Prone to oxidation to methemoglobin, leading to cyanosis.

Genetics and Mechanisms

  1. Mutation Types:
    • Point mutations (most common).
    • Small deletions (e.g., hemoglobin Gun Hill).
    • Tandem duplications (e.g., hemoglobin Fairfax).
    • Frame shifts or elongated β chains.
  1. Inheritance:
    • Usually heterozygous; homozygosity is rare and may present more severely.
    • Approximately one-third are de novo mutations.

Laboratory Findings

  1. Blood Film:
    • Irregularly contracted cells, keratocytes, and polychromatic macrocytes.
    • Possible basophilic stippling and Howell–Jolly bodies.
  1. Hemoglobin Electrophoresis:
    • May show abnormal bands or degraded hemoglobin peaks.
  1. Special Tests:
    • Positive heat or isopropanol instability tests.
    • Increased reticulocyte count due to compensatory erythropoiesis.
  1. Variable Proportion:
    • The proportion of unstable hemoglobin in circulation depends on synthesis and degradation rates.

Clinical Management

  • Splenectomy for severe hemolysis, though it may lead to thrombotic complications.
  • Hydroxyurea to increase fetal hemoglobin.
  • Avoidance of oxidative stress and prompt treatment of intercurrent infections.

Hemoglobin Köln

Mild-to-moderate hemolysis, jaundice, splenomegaly

Weakens subunit interactions, leading to hemoglobin instability and hemolysis.

Mild hemolysis, occasional splenomegaly

Destabilized hemoglobin tetramer with abnormal precipitation and cell membrane damage.

Hemoglobin Lepore

Deletion/fusion of β and δ globin genes

Mixed thalassemia-like phenotype, moderate hemolysis, mild anemia

Fusion results in unstable hemoglobin with reduced oxygen affinity and tetramer instability.

Q. What is the mechanism for polycythemia in high affinity and oxidizing hemoglobins?

 

●      Greater inherent affinity for oxygen than normal adult hemoglobin reduces oxygen delivery to the kidneys → causing increased erythropoietin production and a resultant polycythemia.

 

What % of total Hb do alpha chain variants usually comprise?

●      25%

●      Increases in % if there are concomitant alpha gene deletions

 

Q. What are 4 hemoglobins with increased oxygen affinity leading to polycythemia?

●      Hemoglobin Chesapeake

●      Hemoglobin Heathrow

●      Hemoglobin Kempsey

●      Hemoglobin Bethesda

●      Think of ruddy (red = polycythemia) faced British grannies having a tea party

 

 

Q. What are 4 hemoglobins with increased tendency to oxidation (Fe3+) leading to methaemoglobin formation and cyanosis?

●      Normal affinity

○      M-Saskatoon

○      M-Hyde Park

●      Decreased affinity

○      M-Iwate

○      M-Boston

 

Q. What 2 hemoglobin variants (not thalassemia) have reduced rate of synthesis leading to thalassemic indices?

●      Hb E

●      Hb Lepore

 

Q. What are 3 examples of hemoglobins with a neutral charge that coelute with A on HPLC?

●      New York

●      Koln (? CAP says Koln elutes in HbC window)

●      Bethesda

●      Hammersmith

●      Little Rock

 

Q. What is HbF in homozygous delta beta thal?

●      Homozygosity for some of these deletions causes mild thalassemia intermedia with hemoglobin concentrations of 10 to 13 g/dL and only mild hepatosplenomegaly. Hemoglobin consists of 100 percent HbF.

 

Q. What is hemoglobin A1c?

●      Glucose becomes irreversibly attached to hemoglobin (glycosylation) during the life of the red cell at a rate dependent upon the prevailing blood glucose.

●      The average amount of glycated hemoglobin changes in a dynamic way, reflecting the mean blood glucose over the previous six to eight weeks.

●      This minor component differs from HbA only at the N-terminal amino group of each beta chain, in which glucose is attached nonenzymatically by a ketoamine linkage

 

Q. What is the normal amount of glycated hemoglobins present?

●      Normally A1c represents around 3%

●      There are others that cannot be detected by HPLC.

●      ~5% of hemoglobin molecules have glucose linked to certain lysine residues.

●      These adducts cannot be separated from unmodified hemoglobins by ordinary chromatography or electrophoresis.

 

Q. What is the main issue with calculating A1c in patients with hemoglobin variants?

●      Issue: Interferes with accurate quantification

●      Will be slightly inaccurate as the glycated fraction of the variant is often not captured

●      Some variants cause spuriously low HbA1c, esp slow eluting variants like HbS & C

●      Some variants cannot be glycated (like hemoglobin Raleigh)

●      Some have the same retention time of A1c which causes overestimation of glycated hemoglobin and makes calculation impossible.

 

Q. What 3 hemoglobins cause irregularly contracted cells?

●      C

●      E

●      Unstable Hbs

Q. What 3 hemoglobins have reduced oxygen affinity leading to anemia?

●      S

●      Kansas

●      Titusville

 

Q. What is an extremely unstable hemoglobin leading to a thalassaemic phenotype?

●      Hemoglobin Terre Haute

 

Q. What is hemoglobin Olmstead?

●      An unstable hemoglobin that is a beta chain variant.

●      Causes increased sulphemoglobin

 

Q. Why is hemoglobin Constant Spring severely thalassemic?

●      The hemoglobin itself is functional and relatively stable.

●      The issue is the mRNA is very unstable so only 1-5% of the normal production of the alpha chain is produced

●      Homozygous: Hb ~100 with low-normal MCV, therefore “more anemic than MCV shows”

 

Q. What are the acquired and congenital causes of elevated methemoglobin

1)     Inherited

a)     Hemoglobinopathies

                                             i)          Hemoglobin M disease

(1)  M-Saskatoon, M-Hyde park, M-Iwate, M-Milwaukee, M-Boston

b)     Enzymopathies

                                             i)          Cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency

                                            ii)          NADPH diaphorase deficiency (methemoglobin reductase)

                                          iii)          G6PD deficiency

                                          iv)          Pyruvate kinase deficiency

2)     Acquired

a)     Drugs

                                             i)          Local anesthetic agents → prilocaine and benzocaine

                                            ii)          ABx → sulfonamides, dapsone

                                          iii)          Amyl nitrite, chloroquine,, nitrates, nitrites, nitroglycerin, nitroprusside, phenacetin, phenazopyridine, primaquine, quinones

b)     Environmental agents

                                             i)          Aromatic amines (e.g. p-nitroaniline)

                                            ii)          Chlorobenzene

                                          iii)          Nitrates/nitrites

                                          iv)          Pregnant women are considered vulnerable to exposure of high levels of nitrates in drinking water

                                           v)          Children younger than 4 months exposed to various environmental agents

Distinguish between Type 1 and Type 2 Congenital Methemoglobinemia (NADPH Cytochrome B5 reductase deficiency)

-        Type I - RBC only

-        Type II - All tissues

 

Q. What hemoglobins can cause polychromasia?

●      Hemolysis as a result of unstable hemoglobins or hemoglobin H disease

 

Rarely Reported Hemoglobinopathies

  1. Hb I
    • Cause: Single α-globin substitution (lysine at position 16 replacing glutamic acid).
    • Clinically insignificant unless associated with α-thalassemia (when approximately 70% of hemoglobin is Hb I).
  2. Hb J
    • Characterized by: A fast-moving band on hemoglobin electrophoresis, closest to the anode.
    • Over 50 variants have been reported, including Hb J Cape Town and Hb J Chicago.
    • Clinically insignificant in heterozygous individuals.
  3. Hb Hope
    • Cause: Substitution of aspartic acid for glycine at position 136 of the β-chain.
    • Clinically insignificant, though rare.
  4. Unstable Hemoglobins (these are detected via the isopropanol test, which is positive for unstable hemoglobins):
    • Hb Koln
    • Hb Hasharon
    • Hb Zurich
    • These variants tend to cause unstable hemoglobin.
  5. Other Rare Variants Associated with Erythrocytosis:
    • Hb Malmo
    • Hb Andrew
    • Hb Minneapolis
    • Hb British Columbia
    • Hb Kempsey
    • These variants are rare and often lead to erythrocytosis, where there is an abnormal increase in red blood cell production.

Summary of Important Variants

  • Hb I, J, Hope: Usually clinically insignificant unless associated with other conditions like α-thalassemia.
  • Unstable Hemoglobins (Koln, Hasharon, Zurich): Identified through positive isopropanol test, indicating hemoglobin instability.
  • Erythrocytosis Hemoglobins: Rare, and often associated with increased red blood cell count.

 

Name 2 tests for unstable Hbs

●      Isopropanol stability test

○      Principle-

■      When haemoglobin is dissolved in a solvent such as isopropanol, which is less polar than water, the hydrophobic van der Waals bonds are weakened and the stability of the molecule is decreased.

○      Advantage –

■      Does not require a 37°C waterbath

■      Positive controls can be made by modification of the reagent buffer

○      Interpretation –

■      A normal sample will remain clear until 30 min, when a slight cloudiness may appear.

■      Some unstable haemoglobins will show clearly observable precipitation even after 5 min incubation, whereas milder variants will not show precipitation until 20 min.

○     

●      Heat stability test

○      Principle –

■      When haemoglobin in solution is heated, the hydrophobic van der Waals bonds are weakened and the stability of the molecule is decreased.

■      Under controlled conditions, unstable haemoglobins precipitate, whereas stable haemoglobins remain in solution.

○      Method –

■      Add 0.2 ml of lysate, to a tube containing 1.8 ml of buffer. The negative control is obtained from a fresh normal sample.

■      Place the tubes in a waterbath at 50°C. Examine the tubes at 60, 90 and 120 min for precipitation.

○      Interpretation and Comments –

■      A major unstable haemoglobin will have undergone marked precipitation at 60 min and profuse flocculation at 120 min. The normal control may show some (fine) precipitation at 60 min, but this should be minimal.

What are the causes of increased concentration of sulfhemoglobin?

 

Inherited

  • Autosomal dominant inherited sulfhemoglobinaemia
  • As a feature of some unstable haemoglobins, e.g., hemoglobin Olmstead

Acquired

  • Exposure to drugs and chemicals (as for methemoglobinemia)
  • Sulphur-containing ointments
  • Occupational exposure to hydrogen sulphide
  • Septicaemia (in a neonate)

 

Delta thalassemia. What is the clinical significance?

·        as it only affects the synthesis of hemoglobin A2, is of no clinical significance

·        inheritance of d thalassemia in cis or in trans to b thalassemia means that the hemoglobin A2 will not be elevated and the diagnosis of b thalassemia heterozygosity may be missed

Q: What is Gamma thalassemia, and what is a recognized genetic cause of this condition?

·        G thalassaemia is a condition characterized by a reduced rate of synthesis of the γ (gamma) chain, leading to decreased hemoglobin F production. It manifests primarily during intrauterine life.

·        Minor clinical sequalae because there are four γ genes

Hb Hope

·        Mutation: β136(H14)Gly → Asp (GGT > GAT).

·        Detection: Identified by HPLC (retention time 1.3–1.4 minutes) and CE (zone 10).

·        Effect on HbA2: Causes elevated HbA2 levels, potentially leading to a misdiagnosis of β-thalassemia trait.

·        Diagnostic Considerations: Elevated HbA2 (>4%) in Hb Hope may coelute with HbA2, making it crucial to use other diagnostic methods, including molecular analysis, to confirm Hb Hope and rule out β-thalassemia.

·        Hb Hope can co-exist with other hemoglobinopathies such as α-thalassemia or β-thalassemia.

o   In cases where Hb Hope coexists with other hemoglobinopathies, such as β-thalassemia or α-thalassemia, the clinical presentation could include mild anemia or microcytic anemia, even though Hb Hope itself is usually asymptomatic.

Hb S/Hope

Hb Köln(Koln)

Genetics:

·       Mutation: Beta-globin gene, Valine → Methionine at position 98.

·       Inheritance: Autosomal dominant.

Pathophysiology:

·       Unstable hemoglobin damages RBCs, causing hemolysis and Heinz body formation.

Laboratory Findings:

·       Mild anemia (Hb ~10 g/dL), high reticulocyte count (~32%).

·       Abnormal RBC shapes on smear, positive unstable hemoglobin tests.

·       Elevated ferritin due to iron overload.

·       Hb Köln levels: ~5–30%. Normal HbA/HbA2, though HbA may be slightly reduced.

Clinical Presentation:

·       Chronic mild anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly.

·       Symptoms worsen with infections.

Management:

·       Supportive care: Blood transfusions, iron chelation.

·       Avoid splenectomy unless essential.

·       Regular monitoring for anemia and iron overload.

Special Features:

·       High oxygen affinity without erythrocytosis, easy heme dissociation.

·       RBCs exhibit oxidative stress and reduced deformability, promoting hemolysis.

·       Pulse oximetry may be unreliable due to partial heme deficiency.

Hb Hofu

Genetics:

·       Mutation in the beta-globin gene at codon 126 (T→A), resulting in valine to glutamic acid substitution.

·       Co-inheritance with alpha-thalassemia or beta-thalassemia is possible.

Clinical Presentation:

·       Most cases are asymptomatic.

·       Symptoms in some include mild anemia, headaches, fainting, and blurred vision.

·       Severe anemia requiring transfusions reported when co-inherited with beta-thalassemia.

Laboratory Findings:

·       HPLC shows an unknown peak near HbA0 (~20–25%).

·       Co-inheritance with HbS or thalassemia alters HPLC patterns, sometimes with elevated HbA2.

Q. What are the classifications of hemoglobin disorders?

They can be grouped into three main categories:

  1. Those owing to structural variants of haemoglobin, such as Hb S.
  2. Those owing to failure to synthesize one or more of the globin chains of haemoglobin at a normal rate, as in the thalassaemias.
  3. Those owing to failure to complete the normal neonatal switch from fetal haemoglobin (Hb F) to adult haemoglobin (Hb A). Referred to as hereditary persistence of fetal haemoglobin (HPFH).

•        An individual can also have a combination of two or more of these abnormalities

 

Q. How many genes for fetal hemoglobin are there?

●      2 → the two gamma-globin genes HBG2 and HBG1 (gamma-A, gamma-G)

 

Q. What is the definition of an increased hemoglobin F percentage beyond infancy?

·        >1%

·        Some use >2%

 

Q. What are general genetic causes of HPFH - name 5?

  1. Sickle cell anemias
  2. Beta thalassemias
  3. Delta beta thalassemias
  4. Deletional HPFH
  5. Non-deletional HPFH

 

Q. What is the difference between HPFH and delta beta and delta beta0 thalassemia?

·        HPFH is caused by mutations within the beta globin gene cluster that alter normal hemoglobin switching. Heterozygous shows 30% HbF with normal indices and homozygous or compound heterozygous shows 100% HbF with mild erythrocytosis.

·        Delta beta thal is caused by a deletion in both the delta and beta genes on chromosome 11. The gamma genes on the affected chromosome increase their production of gamma globin and thus increase the HbF. Heterozygous shows as thalassemia minor and homozygous shows thalassemia intermedia with a mild anemia.

·        HPFH has 15-30% HbF and almost balanced alpha and beta globin chain synthesis

·        Delta beta0 thal has 5-15% HbF and unbalanced chain synthesis

 

Q. What are the causes of HPFH?

·        Deletional: deletions within the globin cluster or from mutations or polymorphisms of regulatory genes

·        Nondeletional: polymorphism in regulatory sequences of the beta globin gene cluster

Q. What is the cause of delta-beta thal?

●      Large deletions → in the HBB gene cluster that remove the beta- AND delta-globin genes, sparing both gamma-globin genes or HBG2 (?G gamma) alone cause delta beta thalassemia.

●      Result is increase in Hb F (Presumably because there is decreased beta and delta chains, so the alpha needs some partner… only one left is Gamma!)

Note: Chromosome 11 contains Beta gene, 16 contains alpha

Q. How do the clinical phenotypes of homozygous HPFH and homozygous delta-beta thalassemia differ and why?

 

·        HPFH: asymptomatic; balanced alpha to non-alpha chain synthesis (large deletions lead to loss of delta and beta genes and promoter regions so beta gene is never “turned on”)

·        Homozygous Delta-beta: thalassemia intermedia due to imbalance of alpha to non-alpha chain

Hereditary Persistence of Fetal Hemoglobin (HPFH) and δβ-thalassemia are genetic disorders characterized by elevated levels of fetal hemoglobin (HbF) in adulthood. Deletions of variable sizes, and at different positions, that involve the β-globin gene complex on chromosome 11 are associated with these disorders. The distinction between these conditions is made based on clinical and hematological data. Deletional HPFH includes a wide range of conditions, but typically it is characterized in heterozygotes by levels of HbF of 15% to 30% with normal red blood cell indices, while heterozygotes for δβ-thalassemia tend to have elevated levels of HbF that are lower (5% to 20%) and accompanied by mild anemia with hypochromic, microcytic red blood cell indices.

Q. Provide 3 inherited causes of ~100% Hb F in an adult?

1.     Beta thal major (also with increased A2, microcytic anemia)

2.     Homozygous HPFH (all F, no A2 or A, normal CBC)

3.     Homozygous delta-beta (low A2, microcytic anemia)

Q. What are the clinical consequences of HPFH and delta beta thal?

·       Heterozygous db-thal is asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic

·       Homozygous db-thal can cause severe anemia resembling beta thal intermedia

·       Increased HbF is protective in patients with Hbs-HPFH

Acquired HBH disease

Alpha thal may be subdivided into 3 main etiological categories, such as:

·       Inherited alpha thal syndromes

·       Alpha thal mental retardation syndrome (ATRX)

·       Acquired HbH disease (most common form of acquired alpha thal)

Q. What gene is involved in acquired hemoglobin H disease

 

●      Mutations affecting the ATRX gene on the X chromosome

●      Somatic (acquired) mutations of this locus appear to account for at least some of the cases of acquired alpha thalassemia that can be seen in MDS, AML, and MPNs.

 

Acquired disorders of globin chain synthesis may result from what 3 processes?

 

1)     Mutation of a globin gene

2)     Altered methylation status of a globin gene leading to altered expression; or

3)     The influence of other genes on the expression of globin genes.

●      Acquired somatic mutations of globin genes are very rare.

●      Altered expression is much more common.

●      Post-translational modification of hemoglobin structure can also occur as a result of inherited abnormalities, other than those of globin genes, or as a result of exposure to toxic drugs or chemicals

 

Q. Most common phenotype for acquired thalassemia?

 

●      Acquired HbH disease

●      Less commonly alpha thal trait, beta or delta-beta thal

 

Q. 3 conditions associated with acquired HbH disease?

 

●      MDS eg MDS with single lineage dysplasia & RS (ATMDS acquired thalassemia MDS)

●      AML eg erythroleukemia (M6)

●      MPN eg PMF

●      MDS/MPN eg atypical CML

 

Q. Most common cause of acquired HbH disease?

 

●      Transacting modifier leading to downregulation of structurally normal globin genes

●      Somatic mutation of ATRX gene

●      More common in males (>90% -> X-lined)

 

Q. Four features of acquired HbH that differ from inherited form?

 

●      Microcytosis may be absent

●      Dimorphic RBC population

●      The % of HbH is higher

○      Variable → from a few % to 60-65% (higher than inherited HbH)

●      Symptoms are more severe

○      Sx often more severe than would be expected for degree of anemia

○      Sx more severe in acquired ATRX mutations than constitutional ATRX mutations too

Q. What are the 3 clinical features of the ATR-X syndrome?

 

●      Hemoglobin H disease is relatively mild and the clinical presentation is dysmorphism and mental retardation in young boys.

●      There is short stature, microcephaly, facial dysmorphism and abnormalities of the external genitalia.
